questions.stem: When execution stops at a breakpoint, the highlighted current statement has generally not executed yet. What can you do at that point?

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft Visual Studio documentation, First look at the debugger: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/debugger/debugger-feature-tour?view=visualstudio. A breakpoint suspends execution so current state can be inspected before stepping onward.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft Visual Studio documentation, First look at the debugger: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/debugger/debugger-feature-tour?view=visualstudio. A breakpoint suspends execution so current state can be inspected before stepping onward.

questions.solution: A breakpoint suspends execution so current state can be inspected before stepping onward.

choices.text: Inspect current program state before executing that statement
Only edit the Git commit message
Assume every local already has its post-statement value

questions.stem: Which debugger action normally runs until the next breakpoint, break event, exception, or program completion?

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft Visual Studio documentation, First look at the debugger: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/debugger/debugger-feature-tour?view=visualstudio. Continue resumes normal execution until another stopping condition.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft Visual Studio documentation, First look at the debugger: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/debugger/debugger-feature-tour?view=visualstudio. Continue resumes normal execution until another stopping condition.

questions.solution: Continue resumes normal execution until another stopping condition.

questions.stem: Put these actions in the most sensible order for observing a variable assignment in the debugger.

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft Visual Studio documentation, First look at the debugger: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/debugger/debugger-feature-tour?view=visualstudio. Set breakpoint before/at assignment, run to it, inspect pre-state, step the assignment, inspect post-state.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft Visual Studio documentation, First look at the debugger: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/debugger/debugger-feature-tour?view=visualstudio. Set breakpoint before/at assignment, run to it, inspect pre-state, step the assignment, inspect post-state.

questions.solution: Set breakpoint before/at assignment, run to it, inspect pre-state, step the assignment, inspect post-state.

metadata.note: Ordering schema uses listed order as answer

items: Set a breakpoint before or on the assignment
Step over/into the assignment as appropriate

questions.stem: In C#, what is the value of `15 / 4` when both operands are `int`?

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft C# reference, Arithmetic operators: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/arithmetic-operators. For integer operands, `/` performs integer division; 15 / 4 is 3.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft C# reference, Arithmetic operators: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/arithmetic-operators. For integer operands, `/` performs integer division; 15 / 4 is 3.

questions.solution: For integer operands, `/` performs integer division; 15 / 4 is 3.

choices.rationale: Integer division discards the fractional remainder.
That requires a floating-point operand/result.
Integer division does not round to nearest.

questions.stem: What does `15 % 4` evaluate to for integer operands?

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft C# reference, Arithmetic operators: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/arithmetic-operators. The remainder after 15 / 4 is 3.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft C# reference, Arithmetic operators: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/arithmetic-operators. The remainder after 15 / 4 is 3.

questions.solution: The remainder after 15 / 4 is 3.

questions.stem: Parentheses can be used to make the intended grouping of an arithmetic expression explicit even when operator precedence would already give the same result.

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft C# reference, Arithmetic operators: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/arithmetic-operators. Parentheses explicitly control or document grouping.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft C# reference, Arithmetic operators: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/arithmetic-operators. Parentheses explicitly control or document grouping.

questions.solution: Parentheses explicitly control or document grouping.

questions.stem: Which .NET type is the C# keyword `int` an alias for?

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft C# reference, Integral numeric types: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/integral-numeric-types. `int` is the alias for signed 32-bit `System.Int32`.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft C# reference, Integral numeric types: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/integral-numeric-types. `int` is the alias for signed 32-bit `System.Int32`.

questions.solution: `int` is the alias for signed 32-bit `System.Int32`.

questions.stem: In `int age = 7;`, what is the role of `=`?

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft C# language specification, Variables: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/variables. The initializer assigns the value 7 to the local variable.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft C# language specification, Variables: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/variables. The initializer assigns the value 7 to the local variable.

questions.solution: The initializer assigns the value 7 to the local variable.

questions.stem: Evaluate the C# integer expression `2 + 3 * 4`.

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft C# reference, Arithmetic operators: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/arithmetic-operators. Multiplication has higher precedence than addition: 2 + (3*4) = 14.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft C# reference, Arithmetic operators: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/arithmetic-operators. Multiplication has higher precedence than addition: 2 + (3*4) = 14.

questions.solution: Multiplication has higher precedence than addition: 2 + (3*4) = 14.

questions.stem: Evaluate the C# integer expression `(2 + 3) * 4`.

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft C# reference, Arithmetic operators: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/arithmetic-operators. Parentheses force 2+3 first, then multiply by 4.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft C# reference, Arithmetic operators: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/arithmetic-operators. Parentheses force 2+3 first, then multiply by 4.

questions.solution: Parentheses force 2+3 first, then multiply by 4.

questions.stem: For integer operands, evaluate `17 / 5 * 5 + 17 % 5`.

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft C# reference, Arithmetic operators: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/arithmetic-operators. 17/5 is 3, 3*5 is 15, 17%5 is 2, total 17. This reconstructs dividend = quotient*divisor + remainder.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft C# reference, Arithmetic operators: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/arithmetic-operators. 17/5 is 3, 3*5 is 15, 17%5 is 2, total 17. This reconstructs dividend = quotient*divisor + remainder.

questions.solution: 17/5 is 3, 3*5 is 15, 17%5 is 2, total 17. This reconstructs dividend = quotient*divisor + remainder.

questions.stem: Which literal has type `float`?

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft C# reference, Floating-point numeric types: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/floating-point-numeric-types. A real literal with `f` or `F` suffix is `float`; unsuffixed real literals are `double`.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft C# reference, Floating-point numeric types: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/floating-point-numeric-types. A real literal with `f` or `F` suffix is `float`; unsuffixed real literals are `double`.

questions.solution: A real literal with `f` or `F` suffix is `float`; unsuffixed real literals are `double`.

questions.stem: C# `long` becomes a 32-bit type when the program runs on a 32-bit operating system.

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft C# reference, Integral numeric types: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/integral-numeric-types. C# `long` is always `System.Int64`; native-sized `nint`/`nuint` depend on process architecture.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft C# reference, Integral numeric types: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/integral-numeric-types. C# `long` is always `System.Int64`; native-sized `nint`/`nuint` depend on process architecture.

questions.solution: C# `long` is always `System.Int64`; native-sized `nint`/`nuint` depend on process architecture.

questions.stem: What is the range of C# `byte`?

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft C# reference, Integral numeric types: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/integral-numeric-types. `byte` is an unsigned 8-bit integer: 0..255.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft C# reference, Integral numeric types: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/integral-numeric-types. `byte` is an unsigned 8-bit integer: 0..255.

questions.solution: `byte` is an unsigned 8-bit integer: 0..255.

questions.stem: What is the range of C# `sbyte`?

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft C# reference, Integral numeric types: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/integral-numeric-types. `sbyte` is signed 8-bit: -128..127.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft C# reference, Integral numeric types: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/integral-numeric-types. `sbyte` is signed 8-bit: -128..127.

questions.solution: `sbyte` is signed 8-bit: -128..127.

questions.stem: A C# `char` is always one complete user-perceived character.

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft .NET documentation, Character encoding in .NET: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/base-types/character-encoding-introduction. `char` is one UTF-16 code unit; some Unicode scalar values and grapheme clusters require multiple code units.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft .NET documentation, Character encoding in .NET: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/base-types/character-encoding-introduction. `char` is one UTF-16 code unit; some Unicode scalar values and grapheme clusters require multiple code units.

questions.solution: `char` is one UTF-16 code unit; some Unicode scalar values and grapheme clusters require multiple code units.

questions.stem: Why is the statement “converting any `int` to `float` is exact” incorrect?

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft C# reference, Built-in numeric conversions: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/numeric-conversions. C# allows the implicit conversion, but sufficiently large integers can lose precision in `float`.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft C# reference, Built-in numeric conversions: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/numeric-conversions. C# allows the implicit conversion, but sufficiently large integers can lose precision in `float`.

questions.solution: C# allows the implicit conversion, but sufficiently large integers can lose precision in `float`.

choices.text: Some large integer values cannot be represented exactly by `float` and lose precision
A `float` has a larger exact integer precision than every `int` value

questions.stem: In the usual unchecked context, what happens when an `int` operation overflows at run time?

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft C# reference, checked and unchecked statements: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/checked-and-unchecked. Unchecked non-constant integral overflow wraps/truncates; checked context can throw OverflowException.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft C# reference, checked and unchecked statements: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/checked-and-unchecked. Unchecked non-constant integral overflow wraps/truncates; checked context can throw OverflowException.

questions.solution: Unchecked non-constant integral overflow wraps/truncates; checked context can throw OverflowException.

choices.text: The value wraps according to unchecked integral arithmetic
The compiler automatically changes the variable to `long`

questions.stem: C# integral overflow always throws `OverflowException`.

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft C# reference, checked and unchecked statements: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/checked-and-unchecked. It throws for checked run-time integral operations; ordinary unchecked arithmetic can wrap.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft C# reference, checked and unchecked statements: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/checked-and-unchecked. It throws for checked run-time integral operations; ordinary unchecked arithmetic can wrap.

questions.solution: It throws for checked run-time integral operations; ordinary unchecked arithmetic can wrap.

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft C# reference, Integral numeric types: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/integral-numeric-types. sbyte spans -128..127; byte cannot represent negatives; short works but is wider.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft C# reference, Integral numeric types: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/integral-numeric-types. sbyte spans -128..127; byte cannot represent negatives; short works but is wider.

questions.solution: sbyte spans -128..127; byte cannot represent negatives; short works but is wider.

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft C# reference, Integral numeric types: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/integral-numeric-types. byte spans 0..255; sbyte ends at 127; short works but is wider.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft C# reference, Integral numeric types: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/integral-numeric-types. byte spans 0..255; sbyte ends at 127; short works but is wider.

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft C# reference, Floating-point numeric types: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/floating-point-numeric-types. Unsuffixed 10.0 is double and there is no implicit double-to-float conversion. Add f/F suffix.

questions.stem: What is the documented return type of `Console.ReadLine()` in current .NET?

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft .NET API documentation, Console.ReadLine: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.console.readline?view=net-10.0. `Console.ReadLine()` returns `string?`: the next line, or `null` when no more lines are available.

questions.solution: `Console.ReadLine()` returns `string?`: the next line, or `null` when no more lines are available.

questions.stem: In the normal interactive console case, `Console.ReadLine()` waits for input until a line terminator is entered or the input stream ends.

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft .NET API documentation, Console.ReadLine: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.console.readline?view=net-10.0. `ReadLine` reads the next line from standard input and can wait for interactive input.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft .NET API documentation, Console.ReadLine: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.console.readline?view=net-10.0. `ReadLine` reads the next line from standard input and can wait for interactive input.

questions.solution: `ReadLine` reads the next line from standard input and can wait for interactive input.

questions.stem: What does `Console.WriteLine(...)` add after the supplied output?

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft .NET API documentation, Console.WriteLine: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.console.writeline?view=net-10.0. `WriteLine` writes the value followed by the current line terminator.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft .NET API documentation, Console.WriteLine: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.console.writeline?view=net-10.0. `WriteLine` writes the value followed by the current line terminator.

questions.solution: `WriteLine` writes the value followed by the current line terminator.

questions.stem: Standard input is a stream and can be redirected; it is not inherently limited to keyboard input from a console window.

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft .NET API documentation, System.Console: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.console?view=net-10.0. The Console API exposes standard input as a TextReader stream that can be redirected.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft .NET API documentation, System.Console: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.console?view=net-10.0. The Console API exposes standard input as a TextReader stream that can be redirected.

questions.solution: The Console API exposes standard input as a TextReader stream that can be redirected.

questions.stem: The user types `25` and presses Enter. Why can the direct result of `Console.ReadLine()` not be used as an integer operand without parsing/conversion?

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft .NET API documentation, Console.ReadLine: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.console.readline?view=net-10.0. `ReadLine` returns text, not an integer value; numeric text must be parsed/converted before numeric arithmetic.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft .NET API documentation, Console.ReadLine: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.console.readline?view=net-10.0. `ReadLine` returns text, not an integer value; numeric text must be parsed/converted before numeric arithmetic.

questions.solution: `ReadLine` returns text, not an integer value; numeric text must be parsed/converted before numeric arithmetic.

questions.stem: What is true about a local variable declared as `string userInput;` before it has been assigned?

feedback.correct: Correct. Microsoft C# language specification, Variables: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/variables. Local variables must be definitely assigned before their value is read; an uninitialized local is not automatically usable as `null` or an empty string.

Local variables must be definitely assigned before their value is read; an uninitialized local is not automatically usable as `null` or an empty string.

questions.solution: Local variables must be definitely assigned before their value is read; an uninitialized local is not automatically usable as `null` or an empty string.

choices.text: It must be definitely assigned before it is read
It is automatically an empty string

questions.stem: Which operator should test whether the string variable `userInput` contains the value `"2"`?

String escape sequences do not control program termination.

feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft Learn, Strings in C#: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/strings/

questions.solution: `\n` is the newline escape sequence, representing LF in the string. Teaching provenance: F26/TeachingRecord/Week02/analysis/W02D04.

questions.stem: Which statement about a local variable declared as `int x;` is correct in C#?
questions.author: Tim Rossiter

choices.text: It can always be read immediately and is guaranteed to contain 0
choices.rationale: C# definite-assignment rules do not allow normal code to read an unassigned local just because its type is `int`.

choices.text: It must be definitely assigned before code can read it
choices.rationale: The compiler requires a local to be definitely assigned before its value is read.

choices.text: It contains a random value and C# allows the program to read it
choices.rationale: The language prevents the normal unassigned read.

choices.text: The value depends on whether the debugger is open
choices.rationale: Debugger display does not change the language's definite-assignment rule.

feedback.correct: Correct. Check C# language specification, Variables §9.4 Definite assignment: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/variables
feedback.incorrect: Recheck C# language specification, Variables §9.4 Definite assignment: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/variables

questions.solution: Local variables are governed by definite-assignment analysis. Debugger storage display before an initializer executes is not a C# language guarantee. Teaching provenance: F26/TeachingRecord/Week02/analysis/W02D04.

questions.stem: For the beginner Simple Calculator using concepts taught through W02D04, which sequence best describes the operation-selection part?
questions.author: Tim Rossiter

choices.text: Read the operation choice, compare it with menu choices, execute the first matching branch, then display the result
choices.rationale: This matches the prompt/read/compare/branch model taught in W02D04.

choices.text: Run every arithmetic operation and let the user choose which printed answer to keep
choices.rationale: Conditionals exist so the program can select one path rather than execute every operation.

choices.text: Convert the operation choice to a floating-point number before any comparison
choices.rationale: The menu can compare direct string choices such as `"1"`, `"2"`, and `"3"`.

choices.text: Use a loop because conditionals cannot select among menu choices
choices.rationale: Loops repeat work; the current operation selection is handled by conditional branching.

feedback.correct: Correct. Check Microsoft Learn, Selection statements in C#: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/statements/selection
feedback.incorrect: Recheck Microsoft Learn, Selection statements in C#: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/statements/selection

questions.solution: The W02D04 design is prompt/read/compare/branch. Loops were explicitly deferred for this week's assignment. Teaching provenance: F26/TeachingRecord/Week02/analysis/W02D04.
